newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks slide as Liggett strikes settlement.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks slide as Liggett strikes settlement.

text.p: Fearing for the safety of their tobacco holdings, investors dumped shares on Thursday as Liggett Group Inc, the smallest major U.S. tobacco company, announced it struck another legal settlement.
But most financial analysts were steadfast in their belief that the tobacco stocks were undervalued and would withstand the latest assault.
"I don't think we're going to find a smoking gun in Liggett's document file that's going to find the light of day," Smith Barney analyst Martin Feldman said.
Still, at least one analyst, Diana Temple at Salomon Brothers, turned more cautious, cutting her rating on Philip Morris Cos Inc stock to hold from buy.

The market responded in kind. On the New York Stock Exchange, shares in Philip Morris Cos Inc tumbled to 115-7/8, down 6-1/8. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, the parent company of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, fell 5/8 to 31-5/8.
On the American Stock Exchange, the Tobacco Index .TOB dropped 6.79 to 283.66, down 2.34 percent.

It was the second time that Liggett Group, a unit of Brooke Group Ltd, shook investor confidence by reaching an agreement to turn over evidence to lawyers spearheading billions of dollars in lawsuits against the tobacco industry.
Vowing to "break the backs of this conspiracy of deceit by the tobacco companies," attorneys general from 22 states suing the industry announced in Washington that Liggett had folded.

But Wall Street analysts -- joined by comments from Philip Morris -- said the settlement was a bald ploy by Brooke Group's chairman, Bennett LeBow, to coerce another tobacco company to acquire Liggett.

"The only real idea that makes any sense is that (LeBow) is hopeful that, if he is enough of a thorn in the side of the industry, someone will buy him out to shut him down," said David Adelman, Dean Witter's tobacco analyst.
"He knows he's not going to be around for long, and he's trying to force the hand of one of his competitors to buy him out," Adelman said.

Investors are not so sure. Philip Morris, the world's largest tobacco company, a blue-chip stock and Dow Jones industrial average component, has lost about $20 billion in market capitalization value -- in eight trading sessions.
From a 52-week high of 139-3/4 on March 11, the company's stock has dropped about $25 a share as of Thursday afternoon.

No matter whether a Liggett buyout is LeBow's intention, he has precipitated unrest and volatility in the stock market. As a result, many analysts believe, it is only a matter of time before there is an industrywide settlement of litigation and regulation by the U.S. government.

"This will come as a two-step process sometime during the next 12 months," Feldman said. "There will be new congressional legislation dealing with the easier areas of youth access to marketing, health warnings and federal taxes.
"When that has been achieved and you have some of the uncertainty removed, in the industry and the tobacco lobby there will a greater motivation to explore the possibility of a compromise," he said.
Salomon's Temple, in a research report issued Thursday, also said the forces at work would bring the industry closer to a settlement.
"The silver lining...is that a multi-billion-dollar loss would accelerate the settlement process," Temple said in the report.
